newsitem.title: UK: Britain gives Euro minister post to BP head.
newsitem.headline: Britain gives Euro minister post to BP head.

text.p: Britain's new Labour government on Wednesday appointed British Petroleum Co Plc chairman Sir David Simon, a strong supporter of a single European currency, as minister for trade and competitiveness in Europe.
Prime Minister Tony Blair described Simon, 58, as one of the country's most distinguished businessmen and said he would be responsible for pushing through key areas of policy.
"The post that I have created for him is vital to the future success of our country," Blair said.
"It will cover the whole competitiveness agenda in Europe, pushing forward our objectives of completing the single market and spreading flexible labour markets throughout Europe."

Simon will be given a life peerage to allow him to sit in the House of Lords, the upper house of parliament. Labour sources said Simon, who is not a party member, would not be paid a ministerial salary. The appointment suggests the new administration, which wants warmer ties with Europe and Britain to be one of the Big Three in the European Union, is far less hostile to the idea of a single currency than its Conservative predecessor.

Simon has been one of the most prominent advocates of British participation in monetary union. Labour says it is unlikely to join a single currency in the first wave, beginning in 1999, and will only join if it is to Britain's advantage and after a referendum.

In a recent essay entitled "EMU -- the route to a confident, competitive Britain," Simon said a single currency would reduce costs for business and give Britain a better chance of sustaining a sound monetary policy and low inflation.

"The stability stemming from membership of a single currency should reduce British interest rates and thus cut the direct costs of every company which borrows," he wrote in a booklet published by the Centre for European Reform.
He rejected the Euro-sceptic argument that joining a single currency would represent an unacceptable renunciation of national sovereignty and control of monetary and fiscal policy.

"The fact is that this control' has long been shared with the international financial markets," Simon wrote. "We already share sovereignty and accountability willingly in such matters as vital as defence and trade negotiations."

Simon, who has been with British Petroleum since 1961, is widely credited with turning around the company in the early 1990s, when it was struggling under a heavy debt burden and at one stage almost fell into a loss.
He took over as chief executive in 1992, when Robert Horton, now chairman of Railtrack, was ousted in a boardroom coup.
Simon halved the dividend and slashed costs, which helped to revive BP's fortunes and its share price. It is now Britain's third most valuable company by stock market valuation.
Simon will serve as a minister of state in both the Treasury and the Department of Trade and Industry and will also be a member of the cabinet's economic and European committees.
Blair said the appointment "further makes good our pledge to build a modern and dynamic economy in partnership with business."
Simon will be replaced as BP non-executive chairman by Peter Sutherland, a former European Commissioner who is now BP deputy chairman and also chairman of Goldman Sachs International.
